topics: Topological Sort Shortest Path in DAGs
materials.summary: Comprehensive lecture slides covering single-source shortest path algorithms, min-heap implementations, negative edge cycle detection, and DAG linear time relaxation.
materials.sampleExtractedText:
Lecture 8: Graph Traversal & Shortest Path Algorithms.
Dijkstra's Algorithm solves the single-source shortest path problem on weighted directed or undirected graphs where all edge weights are non-negative.
Invariant: When a vertex u is settled and removed from the Priority Queue, dist[u] is guaranteed to be minimal.
Failure Mode: If negative edge weights are present, earlier greedy settlements can be violated by delayed negative paths.
Alternative: Use Bellman-Ford algorithm in O(V * E) time to detect negative weight cycles.
Optimization: In Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), relaxing vertices in topological order achieves single-source shortest path in O(V + E) linear time.

pages.text: Lecture 8: Graph Traversal & Shortest Path Algorithms. Dijkstra's Algorithm solves the single-source shortest path problem on weighted directed or undirected graphs where all edge weights are non-negative.
Invariant: When a vertex u is settled and removed from the Priority Queue, dist[u] is guaranteed to be minimal. Greedy Settlement: Once relaxed into the settled set, dist[u] will never decrease.

Failure Mode: If negative edge weights are present, earlier greedy settlements can be violated by delayed negative paths. Negative Cycles: Cycles with negative sum cause distances to decrease continuously without convergence.

Alternative: Use Bellman-Ford algorithm in O(V * E) time to detect negative weight cycles. Optimization: In Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), relaxing vertices in topological order achieves single-source shortest path in O(V + E) linear time.

Alternative: Use Bellman-Ford algorithm in O(V * E) time to detect negative weight cycles. Optimization: In Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), relaxing vertices in topological order achieves single-source shortest path in O(V + E) linear time.

topics: Disk Block I/O Alignment & High Fanout
Range Scans & Leaf Doubly Linked Lists
materials.summary: Database storage engine architecture notes covering high fan-out B+ Tree indexing, disk page retrieval, leaf node linked list traversal, and concurrency control.
materials.sampleExtractedText:
Lecture 12: Database Storage Architecture & Indices.
Why B+ Trees? Modern storage devices transfer data in fixed disk blocks (typically 4KB to 16KB).
A high fan-out node fits hundreds of keys into one disk page, limiting tree depth to 3-4 levels for millions of records.
Leaf nodes are linked in a bidirectional list, allowing O(1) sequential range query scans once the starting boundary key is located.

pages.text: Lecture 12: Database Storage Architecture & Indices. Why B+ Trees? Modern storage devices transfer data in fixed disk blocks (typically 4KB to 16KB).
Disk Block Alignment & High Fan-Out: A high fan-out node fits hundreds of keys into one disk page, limiting tree depth to 3-4 levels for millions of records.
Range Scans & Leaf Doubly Linked Lists: Leaf nodes are linked in a bidirectional list, allowing O(1) sequential range query scans once the starting boundary key is located.
Concurrency Control & 2PL: Two-Phase Locking ensures serializability (ACID Isolation) across concurrent transaction read/write sets.

questions.question: What are the four necessary Coffman conditions required for a system deadlock to occur?
options: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait
Starvation, Race Condition, Paging, Context Switch
questions.explanation: Deadlock can only arise if all 4 Coffman conditions hold simultaneously: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock.

questions.question: In computational complexity analysis, what distinguishes a greedy algorithm from dynamic programming?
options: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each stage without re-evaluating previous decisions, whereas DP examines subproblems comprehensively.
Greedy algorithms always run in O(N!) factorial time.
Greedy algorithms cannot be implemented iteratively.
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms make a irrevocably local optimal choice hoping for a global optimum. Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems by memoizing states.

questions.question: Why does standard Dijkstra's algorithm fail when a graph contains negative-weight edge cycles?
options: It causes distances to continuously decrease without convergence, violating greedy settlement invariants.
The priority queue becomes corrupted with negative keys.
It visits vertices in random topological order instead of by distance.
It requires adjacency matrices and cannot support negative weights.

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with a Min-Heap (Binary Heap) for a graph with V vertices and E edges?

questions.question: In computational complexity analysis, what distinguishes a greedy algorithm from dynamic programming?
options: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each stage without re-evaluating previous decisions, whereas DP examines subproblems comprehensively.
Greedy algorithms always run in O(N!) factorial time.
Greedy algorithms cannot be implemented iteratively.
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms make a irrevocably local optimal choice hoping for a global optimum. Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems by memoizing states.

questions.question: Why does standard Dijkstra's algorithm fail when a graph contains negative-weight edge cycles?
options: It causes distances to continuously decrease without convergence, violating greedy settlement invariants.
The priority queue becomes corrupted with negative keys.
It visits vertices in random topological order instead of by distance.
It requires adjacency matrices and cannot support negative weights.

questions.question: Which algorithm should be preferred over Dijkstra if the graph is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with possible negative edge weights?
options: Topological Sort Shortest Path in O(V + E)
questions.explanation: In a DAG, vertices can be topologically sorted in O(V + E) time, and relaxing edges in topological order computes single-source shortest paths in linear O(V + E) time, even with negative weights.

questions.question: In Dijkstra's algorithm, what does relaxing an edge (u, v) with weight w actually mean?
options: Checking if dist[u] + w < dist[v], and if so, updating dist[v] = dist[u] + w.
Deleting the edge (u, v) if dist[v] is already shorter.
Swapping vertices u and v in the priority queue.
Normalizing weights by subtracting the minimum edge weight.
questions.explanation: Edge relaxation evaluates whether routing through vertex u provides a shorter path to vertex v than previously known, updating dist[v] and the priority queue accordingly.

questions.question: How does the A* Search algorithm optimize standard Dijkstra's algorithm for finding the shortest path to a single target destination?
options: It uses Fibonacci heaps instead of binary heaps.
It adds an admissible heuristic h(n) estimating the distance from node n to the target.
It converts the graph into a spanning tree before searching.
questions.explanation: A* uses the evaluation function f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is the cost from start to n and h(n) is an admissible heuristic directing the search frontier towards the goal.
